title: Two University of Central Florida researchers compare 2,100 automated-vehicle crashes with 35,113 human-driven crashes and report lower crash odds for automated driving in most matched scenarios, with higher odds at dawn, dusk and in turns
summary: In a Nature Communications study, Level 4 automated driving systems from unnamed makers had lower crash odds than human drivers in most matched scenarios and higher odds at dawn, dusk and in turns.
account: Mohamed Abdel-Aty and Shengxuan Ding of the University of Central Florida's Smart and Safe Transportation Lab assembled 2,100 automated-vehicle crash records that run up to June 2023. The records came from the California Department of Motor Vehicles and from the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration's Standing General Order databases (1,099 SAE Level 4 automated driving systems, 1,001 Level 2 driver-assistance systems). The authors added 35,113 crashes of human-driven vehicles from California's Statewide Integrated Traffic Records System (SWITRS) and fitted a matched case-control logistic regression. The matched model uses 548 California Level 4 crashes. In rain, a Level 4 automated vehicle had 0.335 times the crash odds of a human-driven vehicle. Most pre-crash movements also reduced crash odds. At dawn or dusk the odds of a crash for a Level 4 automated vehicle were 5.250 times those of a human-driven vehicle, and in turning maneuvers they were 1.988 times. The authors attribute the advantages to object detection, precision control and decision-making. They attribute the disadvantages to sensor adaptation to changing light and to limited situational awareness. They name as a limit that they could not analyze which automation level or system was active in each crash. The analysis does not attribute vehicles to specific developers, so no individual maker is credited. The paper was received on 30 September 2023, accepted on 2 May 2024 and published in Nature Communications on 18 June 2024. In September 2025 a University of Wisconsin team reported in Accident Analysis and Prevention that automated-vehicle crashes were less severe and that intersections posed greater challenges for automated vehicles.

display.answer: Both cited sources are the same paper by Abdel-Aty and Ding in Nature Communications of 18 June 2024. The authors draw on crash records from the California Department of Motor Vehicles, the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration's Standing General Order and California's Statewide Integrated Traffic Records System.
The geopolitical implications are unclear.

fields.summary: In a Nature Communications study, Level 4 automated driving systems from unnamed makers had lower crash odds than human drivers in most matched scenarios and higher odds at dawn, dusk and in turns.
fields.account: Mohamed Abdel-Aty and Shengxuan Ding of the University of Central Florida's Smart and Safe Transportation Lab assembled 2,100 automated-vehicle crash records that run up to June 2023. The records came from the California Department of Motor Vehicles and from the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration's Standing General Order databases (1,099 SAE Level 4 automated driving systems, 1,001 Level 2 driver-assistance systems). The authors added 35,113 crashes of human-driven vehicles from California's Statewide Integrated Traffic Records System (SWITRS) and fitted a matched case-control logistic regression. The matched model uses 548 California Level 4 crashes. In rain, a Level 4 automated vehicle had 0.335 times the crash odds of a human-driven vehicle. Most pre-crash movements also reduced crash odds. At dawn or dusk the odds of a crash for a Level 4 automated vehicle were 5.250 times those of a human-driven vehicle, and in turning maneuvers they were 1.988 times. The authors attribute the advantages to object detection, precision control and decision-making. They attribute the disadvantages to sensor adaptation to changing light and to limited situational awareness. They name as a limit that they could not analyze which automation level or system was active in each crash. The analysis does not attribute vehicles to specific developers, so no individual maker is credited. The paper was received on 30 September 2023, accepted on 2 May 2024 and published in Nature Communications on 18 June 2024. In September 2025 a University of Wisconsin team reported in Accident Analysis and Prevention that automated-vehicle crashes were less severe and that intersections posed greater challenges for automated vehicles.
